chunks: Capacitor failure modes. The question: What are some common failure modes of a capacitor?
Capacitors do not all fail the same way. The type decides the failure. Ceramic ones are brittle and crack, usually shorting.
Aluminum electrolytics slowly dry out, losing capacitance and gaining resistance. Tantalum ones can fail short suddenly under a surge and may burn.
Film capacitors are the gentlest. Knowing the type tells you what to prevent.
Think of three household items. A ceramic capacitor is a dinner plate: strong until it is bent, and then it cracks.
An electrolytic is a wet sponge: it dries out slowly, faster when hot. A tantalum is like a fuse that can flare when overloaded: fine most of the time, then sudden when pushed.
The comparison is rough, but it matches how each type tends to fail.
Every 10 degrees Celsius cooler doubles the life, so a capacitor running at 65 degrees Celsius core temperature lasts about 16 times as long as at 105 degrees Celsius.
The core temperature includes the ripple self-heating, so a low-ESR part or a larger part at the same ripple lasts longer.
MLCC: multilayer ceramic capacitor, the small ceramic chip type. Dry-out: the electrolyte in an electrolytic evaporating, which raises ESR and lowers capacitance.
Derating: using a part well below its voltage or ripple rating for margin. Inrush current: a surge into an uncharged capacitor when power is applied.
Thermal runaway: a part heating, conducting more, and heating even more until it fails.
A board flexes during assembly and a 100 nanofarads ceramic on the 5 volts rail cracks. The crack lets the inner plates touch, so the rail shorts to ground and the part heats up.
For an electrolytic, a rule of thumb is that life roughly doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius cooler, so a part run 20 degrees Celsius cooler lasts about four times as long.
That is the whole idea.
"Each type fails differently. Ceramics crack from board flex or thermal shock, usually becoming shorts.
Aluminum electrolytics dry out: the capacitance falls and ESR rises, with life doubling for every 10 degrees cooler, and they can vent from overvoltage or reverse polarity.
Tantalums fail short and can ignite after a surge, so derate 50 percent and limit inrush. Films self-heal and age gently.
I derate voltage and temperature and choose the type by which failure I can tolerate."
